content:
Let \(q=3^{2/(2k-1)}\). Then the recurrence is
\[
a_{n+1}=(q-1)S_n+3.
\]
Thus
\[
S_{n+1}=S_n+a_{n+1}=qS_n+3,\qquad S_1=3.
\]
Solving gives
\[
S_n=\frac{3(q^n-1)}{q-1},
\]
so
\[
a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=3q^{n-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\log_3(a_1a_2\cdots a_n)=n+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\log_3 q
=n+\frac{n(n-1)}{2k-1}.
\]
Hence
\[
b_n=1+\frac{n-1}{2k-1}.
\]
Then
\[
b_i-\frac32=\frac{2i-2k-1}{2(2k-1)}.
\]
So
\[
T_k=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^k(2k+1-2i)+\sum_{i=k+1}^{2k}(2i-2k-1)}{2(2k-1)}
=\frac{k^2+k^2}{2(2k-1)}
=\frac{k^2}{2k-1}.
\]
For \(T_k\in\mathbb Z_+\), we need \(2k-1\mid k^2\). Since
\[
\gcd(2k-1,k)=1,
\]
we must have \(2k-1\mid 1\), so \(2k-1=1\), giving
\[
k=1.
\]
Thus the only possible value is
\[
\boxed{1}.
\]
